blocks.x: The days are shorter, the weather colder, but the art exhibits currently on show in New York City are as exciting as ever. From Surrealist books to comics and 100-year-old dolls on display across Museum Mile and the boroughs, plenty of exhibits are widening the scope of what art can be in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and beyond. Whether you're wandering through the Guggenheim's main rotunda or traversing the quiet gallery spaces at contemporary Amant in East Williamsburg, read on for the best art exhibits to keep on your radar.
Read our complete New York City travel guide here, including our roundup of the best museums in New York City. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

New Museum’s first exhibit since reopening looked at where technology’s taken and is taking us, and its current ones hone in on a single person and place through time. Spanning two floors, Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony is the first solo exhibit of the American artist and cinematographer’s work through four decades. Most notably, his eight-minute videomontage Love is the Message, the Message is Death chronicles the tapestry of the Black experience across the 20th century—its grief, joys, and pain through sampled clips from music videos, newscasts, and sporting events. Head to the second floor for Bowery: Devil’s Mile, which courses through four centuries of the mythic lower Manhattan street’s history and many identities, from a pre-colonial Lenape footpath; to a fin de siècle strip of saloons and dance halls; to a gathering space for Beatniks, punk-, and post-rockers; to the museum’s very own place of residence. Though the so-called Skid Row of New York City has made way for a much tamer crowd, its many lives are displayed through 19th-century sideshow flyers, Jacob Riis’s seminal photographs of the working class, and more.
Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony runs through January 3, 2027. Bowery: Devil’s Mile runs through January 31, 2027.

blocks.x: Taryn Simon's Father Country I Do Love You at the Guggenheim

Taryn Simon’s Father Country I Do Love You begins with a story of a story her father had shared of an intelligence officer he met long ago, then introduces the artist’s own account of meeting an anonymous ex-FBI agent. Through some thousand images, text, video, and sculpture, Simons charts more stories within stories of the many characters, places, and historical events the agent had crossed paths with. All set in the museum’s spiraling—in every sense—rotunda, it’s the largest body of work to debut at the Guggenheim; it may sound absurd, but so is real life.

An artist’s haven among warehouses in East Williamsburg, Amant was thrust into the summer spotlight when its restaurant Zoli opened. Before you get too full off of chocolate cake and distracted by that fish tank centerpiece, though, do spend an afternoon with Sentient Earth, a campus-wide installation that invites 28 artists to interpret what the planet might say to us if it were sentient. Larger-than-life blister pill packs laid out as artifacts, objects more closely resembling industrious mining tools and refuse: The exhibit offers a sobering look at our very real impacts, with bits of humor and undeniable urgency.

Not books with art, but books as art are on display in The Surrealist Book: Tomorrow Lives in Mirrors, looking at the Surrealists’ medium of choice for ideological and formal experimentation; highlights include rare work from André Breton, Max Ernst, and especially exciting photomontages from queer artist Claude Cahun, who toyed with gender through portraiture and poetry and is at last getting due diligence after being largely forgotten throughout the 20th century.
